main.title: E.G.G.: Elemental Gimmick Gear
main.subtitle: A sleeper inside an ancient machine
main.summary: E.G.G.: Elemental Gimmick Gear is Birthday's action role-playing game, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 27 May 1999.

cards.heading: A sleeper inside an ancient machine
cards.text: E.G.G.: Elemental Gimmick Gear is Birthday's action role-playing game, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 27 May 1999. An ancient egg-shaped machine is discovered with a sleeping man inside, beginning a mystery around the ruins of Tokion. Exploration uses hand-drawn environments seen from above, giving the landscape a detailed illustrated appearance. The machine provides the central link between that setting and the player's actions. Moving through the ruins means learning how its capabilities interact with mechanisms and obstacles left by a civilisation whose purpose has become uncertain.

cards.heading: Ruins drawn by hand
cards.text: Puzzles place switches, movable objects and closed passages around the route. Finding the next way forward requires inspecting their arrangement and using the machine to alter it. Racing sections change the task by rolling the protagonist into an egg-like form and sending him along rails against opponents. That movement gives the shape in the title a practical use beyond its appearance. The adventure alternates between working through a room and handling a more immediate movement challenge, keeping the equipment tied to several different kinds of progress.

cards.heading: Another scale for the confrontation
cards.text: Boss encounters switch from the illustrated overhead environments to three-dimensional graphics, changing the presentation when the adventure reaches a major confrontation. The discovery of the ancient machine also explains its place in the wider world: researchers studied it and produced copies for everyday use, long before the ruins became active again. That history makes the equipment both an archaeological object and something familiar to the inhabitants. The visual transition at the bosses gives those confrontations a distinct scale, while exploration returns the player to the carefully drawn spaces where the mystery began.

main.title: Survival Kids
main.subtitle: After the shipwreck
main.summary: Survival Kids is a Game Boy Color adventure about staying alive on a deserted island. A child survives a shipwreck and must find the means to continue, with the player choosing a boy or a girl at the start. Known in Europe as Stranded Kids, the game makes food, water and useful objects central to exploration. The immediate goal is practical before it is heroic: learn what the island provides, discover which items can help and work toward a way of escaping it.

cards.heading: After the shipwreck
cards.text: Survival Kids is a Game Boy Color adventure about staying alive on a deserted island. A child survives a shipwreck and must find the means to continue, with the player choosing a boy or a girl at the start. Known in Europe as Stranded Kids, the game makes food, water and useful objects central to exploration. The immediate goal is practical before it is heroic: learn what the island provides, discover which items can help and work toward a way of escaping it.

cards.heading: Use what you find
cards.text: Collecting an object begins a decision rather than automatically solving one. Items can be combined into tools, so understanding their possible uses becomes part of understanding the island. Exploration also has a cost, because the survivor’s needs continue to matter. A promising route may be worth following only after suitable preparation. This gives ordinary discoveries a strong role in the adventure. Food, water and materials are closely connected to the freedom to travel farther, turning small acts of preparation into meaningful steps toward another possibility.

cards.heading: More than one outcome
cards.text: The adventure allows different endings according to what the player discovers and accomplishes. That structure makes the island more than a fixed sequence of obstacles with a single solution. A later attempt can draw on earlier knowledge while following another route through its possibilities. Survival Kids establishes the resourceful approach that would later continue in the Lost in Blue series. On a small handheld screen, it finds tension in the relationship between curiosity and necessity: the wish to keep exploring and the need to remain alive long enough.

main.title: Ape Escape
main.summary: Ape Escape is a 1999 platform game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.

cards.heading: Ape Escape
cards.text: Ape Escape is a 1999 platform game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation. The first game in the Ape Escape series, the game tells the story of an ape named Specter who gains enhanced intelligence and a malevolent streak through the use of an experimental helmet. Specter produces an army of apes, which he sends through time in an attempt to rewrite history. Spike, the player character, sets out to capture the apes with the aid of special gadgets.

cards.heading: Gadgets built around the DualShock
cards.text: Ape Escape is played from a third-person perspective. Players use a variety of gadgets to pursue and capture the apes, traversing across several environments. The game's controls are heavily centered around the analog sticks, being the first game to require the use of the PlayStation's DualShock controller. Development of Ape Escape lasted over two years, and was generally focused on adapting to the use of the controller, which was a significant challenge for the development team.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: Ape Escape was met with critical acclaim from critics, with praise particularly directed at the innovative use of the dual analog controls, as well as the graphics and music; the voice acting received minor criticism. The game is widely considered to be one of the greatest on the PlayStation console, and received several re-releases. The game also spawned numerous sequels and spin-offs, beginning with Ape Escape 2 in 2002. A remake, Ape Escape P, was released for the PlayStation Portable in 2005 to mixed reviews.

main.title: Persona 2: Innocent Sin
main.summary: Persona 2: Innocent Sin is a 1999 role-playing video game developed and published by Atlus for the PlayStation.

cards.text: Persona 2: Innocent Sin is a 1999 role-playing video game developed and published by Atlus for the PlayStation. It is the second entry in the Persona series, itself a subseries of the Megami Tensei franchise, and acts as a sequel to the original Persona. The game was re-released in 2011 for the PlayStation Portable. The original version was not localized for western territories; however, the PSP version was released in North America and Europe under the title Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 2 – Innocent Sin.

Innocent Sin takes place in the fictional Sumaru City, focusing on a group of high school students from Seven Sisters High School. The protagonist, Tatsuya Suou, and a group of friends must confront a villainous figure called Joker, who is causing the spread of reality-warping rumors through the city. The group are aided in their quest by their Personas, personified aspects of their personalities. The gameplay features turn-based battle gameplay, where characters use their Personas in battle against demons, and a separate Rumor system, where rumors spread around the city can influence events in the characters' favor.

Development on Innocent Sin began after the release of the original Persona, and retained most of the original's staff. The game carried over the story themes and basic gameplay mechanics of Persona, while changing and improving on some of the mechanics. The characters were designed by Kazuma Kaneko and Shigenori Soejima. The original release was not localized due to staff shortages and concerns over its content. Reception to the game was generally positive for its original release, but reviews were more mixed for its remake due to its age. A sequel, Persona 2: Eternal Punishment, was released in 2000.

main.title: Driver
main.summary: Driver (subtitled "You Are the Wheelman" in North America) is an action driving video game and the first installment in the Driver series.

cards.text: Driver (subtitled "You Are the Wheelman" in North America) is an action driving video game and the first installment in the Driver series. Developed by Reflections Interactive and published by GT Interactive, it was released on the PlayStation on 25 June 1999, and was ported to Microsoft Windows on 1 October 1999, and to Classic Mac OS on 12 December 2000 by Abersoft Limited.

The game, inspired by movie car chases, sees players driving around four real-life cities – Miami, San Francisco, Los Angeles and New York – using a variety of vehicles, with the plot focusing on the work of an undercover police officer, John Tanner, who infiltrates a criminal outfit to investigate their operations, only to discover a plot by their boss to assassinate the President of the United States.

The game proved a commercial hit upon release, and received favorable reviews from critics. Ports for Microsoft Windows and Mac were released on 1 October 1999 and December 2000. A remake for the Game Boy Color, developed by Crawfish Interactive and published by Infogrames was released in May 2000, while versions for iOS and Palm Pre, developed and published by Gameloft, were released on 8 December 2009. The game was re-released on the PlayStation Network on 14 October 2008. The game's success led to further sequels, including Driver 2 in November 2000 and Driver 3 in June 2004.

main.title: Vandal Hearts II
main.subtitle: A tactical journey through a divided country
main.summary: Vandal Hearts II is Konami's PlayStation tactical role-playing game, first released in Japan on 8 July 1999. The player follows a group of characters through a political conflict, travelling between towns and battlefields as the story develops. Its grid-based encounters make position and anticipation central to progress. Moving one member of the party is a decision about what the enemy may do as well as where the ally should stand. The sequel gives the familiar tactical structure a particular uncertainty, asking the player to plan around an opponent who is also preparing to move.

cards.heading: A tactical journey through a divided country
cards.text: Vandal Hearts II is Konami's PlayStation tactical role-playing game, first released in Japan on 8 July 1999. The player follows a group of characters through a political conflict, travelling between towns and battlefields as the story develops. Its grid-based encounters make position and anticipation central to progress. Moving one member of the party is a decision about what the enemy may do as well as where the ally should stand. The sequel gives the familiar tactical structure a particular uncertainty, asking the player to plan around an opponent who is also preparing to move.

cards.heading: A move has to survive the enemy response
cards.text: The battle system links the player's selected action to an enemy action, making prediction part of every exchange. A target may change position, and a seemingly safe destination can become dangerous once both sides have acted. Equipment determines important aspects of a character's capabilities, allowing the party to be adjusted for the next encounter. The player therefore prepares in two ways: choosing the tools carried into battle and learning how to read an enemy's likely response. A useful plan has to account for movement that has not yet happened.

cards.heading: Travel gives the battles their place
cards.text: An overworld map connects towns and combat areas, with many locations available for return visits. Towns provide the intervals in which the party can gather information and prepare, while newly opened destinations carry the story forward. Takashi Takeda designed the game and Hiroshi Tamawari composed its music. North America received it in December 1999, followed by PAL territories in June 2000. Within the tactical role-playing genre, its distinctive contribution is the pressure placed on prediction: the grid is not only a set of current positions but a place whose next arrangement must be imagined.

main.title: Ogre Battle 64: Person of Lordly Caliber
main.subtitle: A captain inside a revolution
main.summary: Ogre Battle 64: Person of Lordly Caliber is Quest’s tactical role-playing game for Nintendo 64. Magnus Gallant begins as a young captain in Palatinus and becomes involved in the country’s revolution. The player organises a battalion into smaller units and sends them across maps in real time, with encounters switching to a closer view of the fighting. Political choices and the people recruited along the way give the campaign several possible outcomes. The army is both the instrument of the conflict and a collection of individuals to develop.

cards.heading: A captain inside a revolution
cards.text: Ogre Battle 64: Person of Lordly Caliber is Quest’s tactical role-playing game for Nintendo 64. Magnus Gallant begins as a young captain in Palatinus and becomes involved in the country’s revolution. The player organises a battalion into smaller units and sends them across maps in real time, with encounters switching to a closer view of the fighting. Political choices and the people recruited along the way give the campaign several possible outcomes. The army is both the instrument of the conflict and a collection of individuals to develop.

cards.heading: Build the unit before the battle
cards.text: A unit contains a leader and up to four other members. Their classes affect attacks, equipment and statistics, while their positions within the formation influence how effectively they perform. Much of the tactical work therefore happens before two units meet. The player needs a group suited to its intended role and a route that brings it to the right confrontation. Characters can change class as they develop, letting the battalion’s composition evolve instead of remaining a fixed set of pieces from the opening missions.

cards.heading: Orders across a living map
cards.text: Missions commonly require the capture of a stronghold or the defeat of a particular enemy unit. The adviser offers suggestions, but the player can organise the approach differently while pursuing the objective. When units encounter each other, their members execute attacks in a closer, semi-real-time battle rather than waiting for individual player commands. The map and the formation thus operate on different scales: one decides where and when to engage, while the other determines what the group can accomplish once the encounter begins.

main.title: Seaman
main.subtitle: A creature that answers back
main.summary: Seaman is Vivarium's virtual-pet simulation, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 29 July 1999.

cards.heading: A creature that answers back
cards.text: Seaman is Vivarium's virtual-pet simulation, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 29 July 1999. The player cares for strange fish-like creatures with human faces, using a microphone accessory to speak to them. Food, suitable conditions and regular attention keep the inhabitants alive as they develop. Designer Yoot Saito makes the aquarium into a place for conversation as well as care. The creature gradually becomes a companion that responds, asks questions and comments on the person outside the screen, giving an ordinary television an unexpectedly uncomfortable inhabitant.

cards.heading: Returning to the aquarium
cards.text: The simulation follows real time, requiring the player to return on subsequent days and check the creatures' condition. A long absence can have consequences, so progress depends on forming a small routine rather than completing a continuous sequence of levels. Speaking into the microphone supplies the company that Seaman needs. Questions may concern the player's birthday, allowing the creature to respond with events associated with that date. The exchange mixes personal details with trivia, making each visit feel like another conversation with an increasingly familiar resident.

cards.heading: A conversation on the console
cards.text: Seaman's blunt remarks give the relationship a comic edge. Keeping a creature alive does not guarantee polite gratitude, and the contrast between its face, voice and aquarium body is central to the effect. The microphone plugs into the Dreamcast controller, turning a hardware accessory into the game's main point of contact. A Japanese PlayStation 2 adaptation followed later. The original remains distinctive for the way its limited daily actions build anticipation: returning means checking on a living thing that may have something new, and possibly unflattering, to say.

main.title: Hybrid Heaven
main.subtitle: Konami · Nintendo 64
main.summary: Hybrid Heaven is Konami's Nintendo 64 science-fiction adventure about a conspiracy involving synthetic humans and a hidden installation beneath Manhattan. Exploration uses a directly controlled character who can move, climb and solve obstacles, while encounters with biological weapons introduce a separate combat system. The mixture gives the underground complex two rhythms. A route through its machinery asks for immediate navigation, but meeting an enemy turns attention toward positioning, stored energy and a choice of techniques whose usefulness grows through repeated practice.

cards.heading: An infiltration with another kind of fight
cards.text: Hybrid Heaven is Konami's Nintendo 64 science-fiction adventure about a conspiracy involving synthetic humans and a hidden installation beneath Manhattan. Exploration uses a directly controlled character who can move, climb and solve obstacles, while encounters with biological weapons introduce a separate combat system. The mixture gives the underground complex two rhythms. A route through its machinery asks for immediate navigation, but meeting an enemy turns attention toward positioning, stored energy and a choice of techniques whose usefulness grows through repeated practice.

cards.heading: Move into position, then choose the technique
cards.text: During combat, the character and opponent move around a restricted area in real time. Once an attack is selected, the action pauses for choices and their resolution before movement resumes. Energy can be saved for combinations, making the decision to strike now part of preparing a larger sequence. Attacks and defensive actions develop through use, with separate statistics for different body parts. The fighter's capabilities therefore reflect the techniques being practised, while injuries can make a preferred approach less reliable in the next exchange.

cards.heading: A body becomes the role-playing equipment
cards.text: The progression system gives punches, kicks and defensive responses the attention that another role-playing game might reserve for a collection of weapons. Improving a particular part of the body changes the options available when the next creature approaches. Released in 1999, the game also offered an unusual widescreen display option for the console. Its hybrid design is most interesting where the two forms meet: the person exploring the facility is also a developing fighter, with each encounter adding another small decision about the kind of body and technique the player wants to build.

main.title: System Shock 2
main.subtitle: Managing scarce resources aboard the Von Braun
main.summary: On August 11, 1999 System Shock 2 was released for Windows in the United States.

cards.heading: A science-fiction horror RPG
cards.text: System Shock 2 was released for Windows in the United States on August 11, 1999. Irrational Games and Looking Glass combined first-person shooting with character development, hacking and scarce resources. Audio logs gradually explain the collapse aboard the Von Braun, while SHODAN's voice remains a threatening presence. Choices about ammunition, abilities and equipment make survival depend on more than the next shot.

cards.heading: First-person combat and character development
cards.text: As in its predecessor, System Shock, gameplay in System Shock 2 is an amalgamation of the action role-playing game and survival horror genres. The developers achieved this gameplay design by rendering the experience as a standard first-person shooter and adding a character customization and development system, which are considered signature role-playing elements. The player uses melee and projectile weapons to defeat enemies, while the role-playing system allows the development of useful abilities. Navigation is presented from a first-person view and complemented with a heads-up display that shows character and weapon information, a map, and a drag and drop inventory.

cards.heading: Audio logs and starting careers
cards.text: The backstory is explained progressively through the player's acquisition of audio logs and encounters with ghostly apparitions. At the beginning of the game, the player chooses a career in a branch of the Unified National Nominate, a fictional military organization. Each branch of service gives the player a set of starting bonuses composed of certain skills, though may thereafter freely develop as the player chooses. The Marine begins with bonuses to weaponry, the Navy officer is skilled in repairing and hacking, and the OSA agent gets a starting set of psionic powers.

cards.heading: Building a science-fiction dungeon crawler
cards.text: Development of System Shock 2 began in 1997 when Looking Glass Studios approached Irrational Games with an idea to co-develop a game. The development team were fans of System Shock and sought to create a similar game. Early story ideas were similar to the novella Heart of Darkness. In an early draft, the player was tasked with assassinating an insane commander on a starship. The original title, according to its pitch document, was Junction Point. The philosophy of the design was to continue to develop the concept of a dungeon crawler, like Ultima Underworld: The Stygian Abyss, in a science fiction setting, the basis for System Shock. However, the press mistook System Shock to be closer to a Doom clone which was cited for its poor financial success. With Junction Point, the goal was to add in significant role-playing elements and a persistent storyline as to distance the game from Doom.
